title: Dietary Fats and Lipids

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of a triglyceride like a hand: the palm is glycerol and the three fingers are fatty acids. Just like proteins are built from amino acid pieces and sugars from little sugar pieces, fats are built from fatty acid pieces attached to that glycerol palm.

### Question 2

Imagine a school bus where every seat is filled with a kid (hydrogen). A saturated fat is a full bus — no empty seats, all single connections. When there are empty seats (double bonds), the fat is unsaturated instead. Factories can fill those empty seats by adding hydrogen, but that is a way of making a fat, not the definition of one.

### Question 3

Straight uncooked spaghetti stacks neatly into a tight solid pile, but bent noodles can't stack and stay loose. Saturated fats are the straight noodles (solid, like butter), and unsaturated fats are the bent ones (liquid, like olive oil).

### Question 4

Your body is like a factory that can build most fat parts but is missing the specific tool needed to add a bend at one far end of the chain. Since it can't make that bend itself, you have to get those already-bent fats (from foods like fish and seeds) delivered ready-made.

### Question 5

Picture delivery trucks in your blood. LDL trucks drop cholesterol off around the body, and if too many pile up they clog the roads (arteries). HDL trucks pick cholesterol back up and haul it to the liver for cleanup — that's why HDL is the helpful one.

### Question 6

Making trans fat is like taking bendy liquid noodles and forcing some of them to straighten out by squeezing in hydrogen. The straightened, twisted noodles pack together into a solid — but that unnatural twist is the harmful trans shape.

### Question 7

Saturated fat is the type that tends to raise the 'bad' cholesterol trucks (LDL). So eating more of it turns the LDL dial up, while swapping in oils from plants and eating fiber turns that dial back down.

### Question 8

Monounsaturated means one bend in the fatty acid, and olive oil is the classic star of that group. Coconut oil and beef fat are the packed-solid saturated types, and hydrogenated margarine has the harmful trans twist — so olive oil is the one you want.

### Question 9

The label can round tiny amounts down to zero, like saying you have 'zero dollars' when you actually have a few coins. On an older package, seeing 'partially hydrogenated oil' in the ingredients was the clue that a little trans fat may still be hiding in there. It does not mean the ingredient list is out of date, that the oil is a healthy omega-3, or that a huge hidden amount is in there, because the rounding rule only hides amounts under half a gram per serving. Foods sold in the U.S. today no longer use that ingredient, but the rounding rule is the same, so '0 g' can still mean 'a very small amount' rather than none at all.

### Question 10

This is a trade where you drop a solid, saturated fat (butter) and pick up a soft, unsaturated one (avocado). You lower the fat that raises bad cholesterol and keep the good plant fats — a win on both sides.

### Question 11

Fat-soluble vitamins are like passengers who can only cross a river by riding in a fat 'boat.' Take away almost all the fat and there are few boats, so the vitamins get stranded and don't make it into the body as well.

### Question 12

Same amount of energy doesn't mean same effect on your body. The trans fat pushes the 'bad' cholesterol up and the 'good' one down, while the omega-3 fat treats your blood vessels kindly — so the kind of fat matters, not just how many calories.
